FOREWQRD

0.1 This Indian Standard ( Part XIX ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 20 May 1982, after the draft finalized by the Air Quality Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council.
0.2 Chlorine gas is primarily a respiratory irritant. It that concentrations above 9 mg/m* in air are readily normal person is so irritating detectable by a of pollu-

0.3 Devices and techniques for determining the concentration tants in the atmosphere are important for the assessment of hazardous levels in the environment. air quality `, establishing tive measures and appraisal of contamination from a process or

` ambient
ameliorasource.

0.4 In the preparation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from the Publication NO. 42215-01-70 ` Tentative methods of analysis for free chlorine content of the atmosphere ( methyl orange method ) ' issued by the American Public Health Association. 0.5 In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS : 2-1960*.

1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard ( Part XIX ) d escribes the details method for measurement of free chlorine in air.

ORANGE

2.1 Principle - The colour of methyl orange solution ceases to vary with acidity near a PH value of 3.0. The dye 1s quantitatively bleached by free chlorine, and the extent of bleaching may be determined colorimetrically. The optimum concentration range is 0.05-I *O ppm in ambient air ( 145 pg to 2 L,OOpg per ms at 25�C and 100 kPa ). NOT:: 2.2 Range It `Is essential to maintain prorer pE

and Sensitivity - The procedure given is designed to cover the range of 5-100 pg of free chlorine per 100 ml of samplmg solution. For a 30 litre air sample, th;s corresponds to approximately 0.05-l .O ppm Increasing the volume of air samples in air which is the optimum range. extends the ran,ge at the lower end, but only within limits, since 50 litre of chlorine free air produces the same effect as about 0.01 ppm of chlorine.

2.3 Linktatmns and Interferences - Free bromine, which gives the Manganese ( III, IV ) interferes in a positive direction. same reaction, in concentrations of 0.1 ppm or above also interferes positively. Negative interference from sulphur dioxide is significant both in solution as well Nitrites impart an off-,colour orange to the methyl as gaseous state. orange reagent. Nitrogen dioxide interferes positively, reacting as 20 percent chlorine. Sulphur dioxide interferes negatively, decreasing the chlorine by an amount equal to one third the sulphur dioxide concentration. 2.4 Predisian and Accuracy - Error due to measurement by this procedure is known to be less than & 5 percent of the amount present. 2.5 Apparatus for measurement at 505 nm, prefer-

2.5.1 Spectrophotometer - suitable ably accommodating 5-cm cells.

2.5.2 Sampling Train - accorc!ing to IS : 5182 ( Part V )-1975" using a large impinger with fritted disc 1 see Fig. 2 of IS : 5182 ( Part V )1975* ] of porosity C ( 70 to 100 i*rn maximum pore diameter ). 2.6 Reagents - Pure chemicals of analytical grade, unless otherwise specified, and distilled water ( see IS : 1070-l'J77t ) shall be employed in These shall not contain any impurities that affect the results the test. of analysis. 2.6.1 Methyl Orange Stock Solution 0.05 Percent - Dissolve 0.500 g of This solution is stable methyl orange in water and dilute to one litre. indefinitely if freshly boiled and cooled distilled water is used.

2.7 Procedure - Assemble the sampling train. Add 100 ml of sampling solution to the impinger and draw a measured volume of air at a rate of l-2 l/min for a period of time appropriate to the estimated chJor:ne concentration. Transfer the solutron to a lOO-ml volumetric flask and make to volume, if necessary, with acidified water. Measure absorbance at 505 nm in 5-cm cells against water as reference.
2.7.1 The volume of sampling solution, the concentration of orange in the sampling solution, the amount of air sampled, the impmger and the length of photometer cell may he varied to needs of the situation as long as proper attention is paid to the ponding changes necessary in the calibration procedure. methyl size of suit the corres-

2.8 Calibration
2.8.1 of 0,005 0.20 ml O,O*5, into the Quickly Prepare a series of six lOO-ml volumetric flasks containing 6 ml percent methyl orange reagent, 75 ml water, and 3 drops ( O-15) of 5.0 N hydrochloric acid. Carefully and accurately pipette 1.0, 5.0 and 9.0 ml of chlorine soJution ( approximateiy 10 ppm ) respective flasks; holding the pipette tip beneath the surface. mix and make to volume with acidified water.

2.8.2 Immediately standardize the 10 ppm chlorine solution by adding 400 ml of chlorine so!ution to a flask containing 1 g potassium iodide and 5 ml glacial acetic acid, and swirling to mix. Titrate with 0'01 iY sodium thiosulphate until the iodine colour becomes a faint yellow. Add 1 ml `of starch indicator solution and continue the titration to the end-point ( blue to colourless ). One millilitre of 0.010 0 N sodium thiosulphate is equivalent to 0.354 6 mg of free chlorine. Calculate the amounts of free chlorine added to each f!ask in 2.8.1. 2.8.3 Transfer the standards prepared in and measure absorbance against micrograms standard curve. 2.9 Calculations Chlorine, where Calculate FV the chlorine 2.8.1 to absorption cells of chlorine to draw the as follows:

2.10 Effect on Storage - The colour of sampled solutions is stable for at least 24 h if protected from direct sunlight, although the presence of certain interferences ( Fe III ) may cause slow colour change.
